title: Connecting watershed data with environmental-flow research
summary: I automated watershed delineation, modeled stream reference status and investigated hydrologic-alteration relationships across Texas ecoregions. The work combines R-based API integration with Python modeling and contributed to a coauthored River Research and Applications paper, while keeping exploratory model-fit curves distinct from validated ecological conclusions.

image.alt: Combined Texas ecoregion mean R squared comparison
image.caption: Original research output: comparison of mean training R² curves across Texas ecoregions. The set of contributing metrics can change with depth.

problem: Environmental-flow research needs to separate natural watershed context from human alteration and understand how hydrologic patterns vary across regions. That requires consistent watershed boundaries, reference-stream information and analysis that distinguishes model behavior from ecological evidence.
contribution: I automated watershed delineation from stream-gage coordinates, developed a Random Forest workflow for reference versus non-reference streams, and explored relationships between hydrologic-alteration metrics and fish response variables across Texas ecoregions. I am a coauthor of the related 2026 paper on reconstructing historical hydrologic alteration.

approach.title: Retrieve watershed geometry programmatically
approach.body: Used R with the Model My Watershed API to submit gage coordinates, check delineation results and save watershed boundaries for spatial analysis.

approach.title: Model reference-stream status
approach.body: Used watershed and stream attributes in a Random Forest workflow. The original notebook used a regressor with rounded binary outputs; the later reusable script uses a classifier with train/test separation and missing-value handling in its modeling pipeline.

approach.title: Explore hydrologic metrics and fish responses
approach.body: Fitted multi-output decision-tree regressions for individual hydrologic-alteration metrics and multiple fish response variables. Repeated the models across tree depths to examine the change in training fit.

approach.title: Compare patterns across ecoregions
approach.body: Averaged the available metric-level R² scores at each depth within each ecoregion. Numerical derivatives identified candidate inflections in the mean curves for comparison, rather than declaring biological thresholds.

outcome: The work produced reusable delineation and modeling scripts, original ecoregion comparison figures and a contribution to a collaborative peer-reviewed publication. The exploratory curves make differences in fitting behavior visible; their purpose and limitations remain separate from the published team-wide hydrologic modeling results.
learning: This project shows a progression from retrieving spatial data through an external API to building and evaluating statistical workflows around it. The documented change from a rounded regressor to a classifier also makes a useful engineering distinction explicit: improving a reusable implementation can change its results, so historical outputs and revised code need separate provenance.
limitations: The displayed tree-depth R² curves use training data and do not establish out-of-sample predictive performance.
Some metrics stop contributing when fitted trees stop growing. The changing set of metrics can affect the mean curve and its candidate inflection points.
Inflections in model-fit curves are not independently validated ecological breakpoints.
The revised Random Forest classifier is not an exact reproduction of the original rounded-regression workflow. Original research inputs are needed to reproduce historical results.
The paper reflects the full author team; its overall performance measures are not presented here as scores from my separate exploratory fish/HIT analysis.

evidence.title: Coauthored research publication
evidence.body: Mark B. Lueders, Ryan A. McManamay, Jay A. Oliver, David Young, Preston Bean and Kevin Mayes. Reconstructing Long-Term Historical Hydrologic Alteration to Support Environmental Flows in Texas. River Research and Applications, first published July 9, 2026. DOI: 10.1002/rra.70172.

evidence.title: Original ecoregion comparison figures
evidence.body: These figures document the exploratory decision-tree analysis. The average is across model scores available at a depth, not across the raw fish observations or hydrologic values.
